Nice selection. Getting over the akwardness of photographing people is a challenge. Tips?

What sets 500px apart from Flickr and Instagram?

It really, really is. I still struggle with it to be honest. A lot of strategies can help.

Shoot with a friend. I'm lucky enough to have a partner who likes to shoot and will happily be dragged downtown. Many times with our young daughter in tow! Now this can make you and the people you're shooting more comfortable. But it can be a distraction both for you and your subjects. People might not notice 1 slr but they tend to notice 2!

Another strategy I try is to fill my head with thoughts on techniques and subject matter so I'm somewhat oblivious. This is obviously distracting and you might be oblivious to something really awesome you're not actively after.

Going to street events works a treat, more people, all not surprised to have a camera going off nearby. Though more intimate and candid shots might be harder to get.

But at the end of the day these ideas don't make up for developing you're own courage and confidence. Which will come a little more with each photo you take. Of course you might not feel it everyday but when you do seize it!

As for Flickr and 500px... well to me 500 is almost a game or contest with the way they attribute scores to your photos and in general much more dramatic and higher quality photos seem to be the norm there (though there are plenty of stinkers!). While Flickr feels a bit slower and much more inclusive, better for lots of work while 500 seems a nicer place to put your nicer photos.

So this means that subscription revenue is a static value that will be divvied up between partners in amount corresponding to their monthly views. That's a rather dangerous precedent for content creators that changes the market from one with no monetary cap into effectively a zero-sum game. It's no longer in a channel's interest for you to watch another channel's content since that detracts from their share of the total subscription pot.

Amazon has recently enacted a similar system with the Kindle Unlimited plan which has drawn much ire from the writing community. I remember reading one author's interpretation of the Unlimited system and what it means for creators:

That said, the thing to actively dislike about the Kindle Unlimited “payment from a pot” plan is the fact that it and any other plan like it absolutely and unambiguously make writing and publishing a zero-sum game. In traditional publishing, your success as an author does not limit my success — the potential pool of money is so large as to be effectively unlimited, and one’s payment is independent of any other purchase a consumer might make, or what any other reader might read.

In the traditional publishing model, it’s in my interest to encourage readers to read other authors, because people who read more buy more books — the proverbial tide lifts all boats. In the Kindle Unlimited model, the more authors you and everyone else reads, the less I can potentially earn. And ultimately, there’s a cap on how much I can earn — a cap imposed by Amazon, or whoever else is in charge of the “pot.” As an author, I won’t be able to ever earn more than Amazon wants me to (especially if Amazon requires my title to be exclusive).

I guess we'll find out how this system hits Youtube partners' bottom lines in a few months. We'll either get our sub boxes filled with frantic cries or satisfied silence.
